prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock based on the magic-wavelength principle and its realization at fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, enabling comparison of neutral-atom clocks at a new level of precision

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep a single-part prize for B012 with Katori and Ye, and the exchange has made my case narrower rather than broader. What I can defend from experience is the physics: at the magic wavelength the differential light shift of the two clock levels cancels, so many atoms are held in the Lamb-Dicke regime with Doppler and recoil effects suppressed, and the statistical gain from interrogating thousands of atoms at once is what makes 1e-18 reachable in practical averaging times. That has been reproduced in several independent laboratories and is checked by clock-to-clock comparison, which is the most stringent reproducibility test I know of in experimental physics. The millimetre-scale gravitational redshift is a measured effect on nature, not only a better ruler. On the chair's question about distinctness, I would word the citation around the lattice architecture and not around metrology in general. The 2005 prize covered the comb and laser-based precision spectroscopy; the 2012 prize covered control of single trapped ions. Neither rewarded the neutral-atom many-body lattice scheme, and the citation should say so by construction. On the second and third questions, I would credit the invention and early strontium demonstration to Katori and the accuracy, systematics control and many-body clock results at the 1e-18 level to Ye, and I would not add a third name. Moving to Ye's group for the headline numbers is what Olsson suggested and I agree. My choice has not changed, but my confidence that the committee can defend it is higher than at the start of round 1, because nobody has found a scientific flaw and the objections are about novelty relative to earlier prizes and about timing.
statement.case_against: The objections I take seriously have not gone away. First, this is a measurement technology, and the fundamental-physics payoffs (varying constants, dark matter searches, relativistic geodesy, a redefinition of the second) are still prospective; I would prefer to reward a result about nature, and I accept that Danielsson and Mehlig have a point when they say the same. Second, the priority record from about 2001 to 2005 is not entirely clean: Katori's proposal and first strontium lattice demonstrations, Lemonde's parallel Hg lattice proposals, and the JILA, SYRTE and PTB contributions overlap in time, and I am working from memory of the literature, not from documents in front of me. Third, ion-clock groups (Al+, Yb+) reach comparable accuracy and are outside the names, and the ultrastable-laser work that limits clock stability is also outside. Fourth, my first place is a specialist's view and my lineage through Hall's laboratory is a real, if indirect, connection; if the committee finds the two-name credit defensible only with a specialist's reading, it should discount my vote for that.

responses.point: B012 is an invention with clean attribution, verified many times at the 1e-18 level, with the citation written narrowly around the lattice-clock concept so that it does not read as a general metrology prize; the 1e-18 and redshift results are Ye's group's.
responses.response: I agree with your wording point and I think it answers most of the repetition concern raised by Mehlig and Pearce. I would take your suggestion one step further in the draft citation: name the magic-wavelength lattice explicitly, and keep the 1e-18 result in the realization clause, so that the invention is credited to the proposal and the realization to the demonstrated accuracy. I do not share your relaxed view that priority is settled by the two names; the record of Takamoto and Katori, Lemonde and the JILA team in 2003 to 2005 is where a challenge would come, and I think the committee should verify it against the publications before the vote and not trust memory, mine included. On timing I side with your argument that the committee decides on demonstrated science; a pending redefinition of the second is a standards-body matter, and the redshift and comparison results already stand.

responses.point: B029 is a discovery by nature, with a robust diffuse flux consistent with KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD and a bearing on the origin of cosmic rays; he accepts the credit problem of three names for a collaboration of hundreds and says he would not block B012.
responses.response: I respect the case that IceCube is a discovery of nature in the sense I said I wanted, and I agree that the diffuse flux is robust against analysis channel. That is why B029 stays on my alternatives list. My difficulty remains the credit: the question for me is who made the decisive contributions to construction, calibration of the ice and the analysis that established the flux, and the file does not tell us. A prize on a collaboration of hundreds needs that evidence, and the committee also has to decide where Baikal and AMANDA sit. If you can show evidence that Halzen, Karle and Spiering are the right three, I would support B029 as a later-year prize and gladly see it as a second part in a future configuration. This year I cannot put it ahead of B012, whose names carry no such unresolved question, and your own statement that you would not block B012 makes me think we are closer than the vote counts suggest.

responses.point: B036 is a prediction-then-confirmation story with independent reproduction in many laboratories and a platform that has opened further moire phases; he names B012 as the more secure choice if the committee wants settled understanding.
responses.response: I take your point seriously, especially that the central observations are stable even though the pairing mechanism is not, and I withdraw any suggestion in round 1 that the field is simply immature. My remaining hesitation is narrower: the experimental credit is spread over Cao, Fatemi and the first-author group, with Dean and Young on the encapsulated samples, and I cannot tell from the record whether Jarillo-Herrero alone is the right experimental name or whether the committee would be choosing between members of one large team. The theory share, MacDonald with or without Bistritzer, has the same problem. You said the clock is the safer choice if settled understanding is the standard; I would say that is the standard I apply, and in a year when B036 has more years of reproduction and an agreed pairing picture it would be a strong candidate. If you want to press B036 now, what I would need to see is a defensible trio that you would put against Cao and Fatemi in public.

responses.point: B012 rests on one simple, general mechanism understood quantitatively, but the 2005 comb prize and 2012 ion-control prize let a skeptic call it an incremental continuation, and a prize might be better timed after the redefinition of the second; B057 is kept as a first alternative.
responses.response: I agree that the overlap is the strongest objection and that the citation must answer it. My answer is that the lattice clock changed what is measured and not only how well: with many atoms in a magic-wavelength lattice the clock became a many-body sample whose systematics and density effects are themselves physics, and that is why the redshift over millimetres can be resolved at all. That is distinct from the comb, which transfers optical frequencies to the microwave domain, and from ion control, which gives a single-ion reference. On timing, I do not think waiting for the redefinition helps: the prize should follow the science, and the science is established. I would still drop the sentence in my round-1 citation about opening a new regime of precision in general, because it invites the metrology objection you raise; the new draft is explicit about the magic-wavelength lattice.

responses.point: B012 should be decided on the demonstrated science and not on a standards-body decision about the second, and the chair asks whether Kroll's lineage through John Hall's laboratory requires a procedural step.
responses.response: On the lineage question, I do not think a recusal is required: I did not work with Hall on lattice clocks, Hall received his prize in 2005 for a different contribution, I have no joint work, funding or company link with Katori or Ye, and the connection is a few months in a laboratory decades ago. I still want it in the minutes, and I would not object if any member wanted me to abstain from the final vote on B012 and let the other seven decide; I would then expect the committee to say that is a precaution, not a finding. On timing I agree with you that the committee should decide on demonstrated science, and I move from my round-1 position of leaving it open to supporting that view.

uncertainties: The priority record for the magic-wavelength concept and the first strontium lattice clocks among Katori, Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and Ye; I am relying on memory and not on documents, and the committee should check the publications before voting.
Whether the committee accepts that the lattice architecture is distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and whether the narrower citation wording is enough to carry that.
Whether the ion-clock lineage or the ultrastable-laser work should be reflected in the citation text, given that the three-person limit leaves no room for further names.
Whether B029 can be given a defensible trio from a collaboration of hundreds, and whether B036 will settle its pairing picture and credit within a few years.
statement.conflict_note: I spent time in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder during my PhD, and Hall was Jun Ye's doctoral advisor. I have no joint work, funding or company interest with Katori or Ye, and I regard this as a lineage disclosure and not a conflict requiring recusal, but I would accept abstaining from B012 if the committee prefers that. I am a rare-earth-crystal and slow-light person and not a clock person, so my first place reflects a specialist's judgement of the experiments. My WACQT role overlaps institutionally with Chalmers, where Göran Johansson works, which would matter only for B051; I have no connection to the other shortlisted candidates.
